@@128392392 <p> In this report , ABIODUN ADEWALE writes on how a groundbreaking recycling initiative at the National Sports Festival in Ogun State aligns with the global innovation of solving the world 's environmental challenges through sports <p> If you 've ever attended a sporting event , chances are you grabbed a bottle of water , a soft drink , or even a quick meal served on disposable plates . <p> But have you ever paused to notice the mountain of waste left behind after a sports event ? <p> To put it into a better perspective , consider Nigeria 's biggest sporting spectacle , the National Sports Festival . Throughout the two-week multi-sport event , depending on your level of involvement , it 's almost certain you 'll go through at least one bottle of water or drink each day . <p> If you were at the 22nd National Sports Festival , tagged Gateway Games 2024 and staged in May 2025 in Ogun State , pause and imagine the numbers . Now multiply your consumption by tens of thousands of visitors who thronged the venues , and then picture the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mega sporting events like the Africa Cup of Nations , the FIFA World Cup , or even the Olympics , and the figures become staggering . <p> For two weeks , Ogun State played host to over 15,000 participants , including 9,940 athletes and officials , who illuminated Nigeria 's biggest sporting spectacle with grit , energy , and an unrelenting passion to excel in 38 different sports . It was the second time the state welcomed the ' Nigerian Olympics ' -- 19 years after its first hosting in 2006 . <p> The games unfolded across 10 venues , spread through Abeokuta , Sagamu , Ikenne , and Ijebu-Ode . From the MKO Abiola Sports Arena in Abeokuta -- the heartbeat of the festival -- the cheers were deafening as athletes chased medals and national pride . But as the contests grew fiercer , so did another reality : the waste . Piles of discarded items -- mostly plastic bottles and other recyclables -- became an inescapable sight , and the careless manner of their disposal told its own troubling story . <p> Everywhere you turned , plastic bottles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scattered around , a by-product of the fact that food and beverages were the hottest-selling items for vendors at every venue . Finding a seat in the stands often came with its own challenge ; athletes who had eaten breakfast or lunch at the venue sometimes left behind their food packs -- popularly called takeaways -- tucked between the seats or even abandoned right on them after emptying the contents into their stomachs . <p> Now , beyond what was bought and consumed casually , imagine the sheer volume of plastic waste generated from feeding nearly 10,000 athletes three times a day over two weeks . That alone amounted to a mountain of disposables . <p> Yet , despite this overwhelming tide of litter , the festival grounds never truly descended into an eyesore . Volunteers in green and blue t-shirts , armed with litter pickers and bin bags , worked tirelessly to clear the waste almost as quickly as it appeared . Alongside them , sanitation officers maintained a constant presence , ensuring no dirt was left to tarnish the hygiene or spectacle of the games . <p> Still @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where does all that trash -- especially the recyclable plastics -- actually end up ? <p> Green milestone <p> The sports festival in Ogun State , was not only a celebration of athletic excellence but also a landmark moment for Nigeria 's growing environmental sustainability movement . <p> For the first time in the history of the event , a structured , large-scale recycling initiative was integrated into the festival -- turning the grounds of the MKO Abiola Sports Arena into more than just a stadium , but a hub for environmental advocacy and green innovation . <p> Led by Orange Strategy Waste Value , an Ogun State-based social project , and backed by the Ogun State Government , the initiative focused on promoting source-level waste separation and recycling behaviour among locals and visitors during and even after the games . <p> " When we got to know that Ogun State would be hosting the 22nd National Sports Festival , we reached out to the Ministry of Environment to present this collection plan , and they encouraged us to go ahead . We reached out to the Ministry of Youth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . We also reached out to the Local Organising Committee , as well , " CEO of Orange Strategy Waste Value , Titilayo Falaiye , told The PUNCH . <p> " When we put out the application for volunteers , we had over 400 responses , and we shortlisted them to 100 . That way , we tried to accommodate as many people as possible , and we created a shift basis for them to work . " <p> The initiative was driven by a team of 100 volunteers who were distributed around the centres to pick plastic recyclables generated by festival goers , athletes and spectators . <p> These individuals worked tirelessly to ensure that recyclables were properly collected , sorted , and transported to the aggregation centre inside the MKO Abiola Sports Arena before they were sent out for recycling at the end of the games . <p> " It is strenuous , especially because of the weather . It is mostly sunny , but I am the kind of person who advocates environmental impact . So , this gave me some kind of purpose , " one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " Spectators and vendors at the venues also made our job easy and difficult at the same time . Some of these vendors hoarded the plastics , and some would keep them for us till we came around their stands . Due to our presence , too , they became very intentional about how they dispose of these plastics . So , as we got along , we did n't even have to convince them before they threw them into our bin bags . " <p> The project also benefited from partnerships with brands that deal in the production of consumables from recyclables , as a way of taking responsibility for the cleanup and reduction of plastic waste in Nigeria . <p> Their involvement also stems from the extended producer responsibility , a legislation developed with support from the United Nations Environment Programme , that will make companies that produce and use plastic packaging responsible for countering plastic pollution . <p> Nigeria is one of a growing number of countries that have embraced this type of legislation . <p> " It gives us so much joy that we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and that would n't be possible without our partners , including Food and Beverage Recycling Alliance , Coca-Cola , Nestle and Nigerian Breweries , which all provided us with different working materials , " Falaiye said . <p> But the effort did n't end with the festival 's attendees . Orange Strategy also activated mini collection hubs across Abeokuta South , targeting economically vulnerable women in local communities . These women were trained and supported to gather recyclable waste within their neighbourhoods and store it in the designated hubs in exchange for cash . <p> Growing crisis <p> If you take a trip around the major cities in Nigeria , you will be forced to wonder if the country 's environmental pollution has hit a new low , especially with the use of plastic for the packaging of food and drinks . <p> Although plastic became substitute to the use of bottles , especially for beverages , which are fondly called soft drinks by Nigerians , these ' takeaways ' and ' disposables ' eventually added to the existing problems , causing significant environmental damage ; from the imbalance created @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the mercy of pollution , which is in turn a public health concern and more recently , affecting climate change . <p> Recently , Lagos and Abia states banned the use of styrofoam , but they are still widely used in the country . <p> According to a report released through the Non-Residential Fellowship Programme of the Nigeria Economic Summit Group in November 2023 , the country is estimated to generate an average of 2.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually , with its commercial capital , Lagos , generating 870,000 tonnes annually . Some of Orange Strategy Waste Value 's volunteers during the Gateway Games <p> Globally , the World Health Organisation says more than 400 million tons of plastic are produced every year and an estimated 19 -- 23 million tons end up in lakes , rivers and seas . However , less than 10 per cent of the world 's annual plastic production is recycled . In Africa , which produces only five per cent and consumes four per cent of global plastic , a growing population and urbanisation are driving an increase in single-use plastic , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ authors of the paper expressed concern about the steady rise of plastic waste with no direct measures to curb it , to a layman , these statistics might not be scary , not even with the worrisome presence of plastic waste on every street . <p> With 80 per cent of these plastics ending up in landfill , they can take up to a staggering 450 years to decompose , and with Nigeria 's population expected to hit 401 million by 2050 , the problem becomes a ticking time bomb . <p> Impact of green sports <p> Numbers often speak louder than intentions when it comes to environmental sustainability . <p> According to the Ogun State Commissioner for Environment , Ola Oresanya , the state braced for an estimated 10,000 metric tons of waste over the two weeks due to the influx of nearly 25,000 visitors . Given that an average person at such events could generate about 0.7 kilograms of waste per day , the anticipated waste surge was massive . <p> From the report of the cleanup , which was shared with The PUNCH , a total of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ operation , marking one of the most impactful sustainability interventions in the event 's history . <p> Sixty per cent of the recyclables , which is 4,558kg , were Polyethylene Terephthalate , which are bottles of water and drinks -- this shows the prevalence of single-use plastics at events of this magnitude . <p> Polypropylene ( bottle tops and fittings ) made up 21 per cent of the volume , which is calculated at 1,593.9kg . That is money for those who are doing recycling . And do n't forget one thing , that we have the highest number of recycling factories in Nigeria . We recycle about 1,500 tons of plastic daily . " <p> Money-making venture <p> Like the commissioner pointed out , indeed , the people of Ogun State took advantage of the opportunity by keying into the monetary value of plastic waste at each stage of its life cycle , including sorting , collection , and recycling . <p> Aside from the formal efforts to protect the planet , hosting the games unlocked economic opportunities through an informal environmental stewardship of young boys and women . <p> At the end of every event-filled day at the MKO Abiola Sports Arena , just before the lights go off , when many spectators took to the field for a dance fest , some boys like Oluwadamilare Lawson , a 17-year-old second school leaver , begin to comb the stands for every PET bottle ( for water or drinks ) that they can find . <p> This happens after volunteers might have also closed for the day , and one of those in the informal initiative could pick at least five full sacks of 50kg rice . <p> " I just come around the venue to pick plastic bottles that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pay for my UTME exam . A volunteer picking plastic during the Gateway Games in Abeokuta . Photo -- Orange Strategy Waste Value <p> In Ojota , Lagos , there is a deep-lying settlement that is synonymous with scraps . @@128392418 <p> The Nigeria Humanitarian Fund ( NHF ) has announced fresh allocations to address rising food insecurity and anticipated flooding across the conflict-affected states of Borno , Adamawa , and Yobe ( BAY ) , where millions face deteriorating humanitarian conditions . <p> Nigeria is facing an escalating humanitarian emergency in the northeast , with conflict , food insecurity , and climate shocks threatening millions of lives . According to the March 2025 Cadre Harmonis ? , about 4.6 million people in Borno , Adamawa , and Yobe ( BAY ) states are expected to face crisis or emergency levels of food insecurity during the peak lean season from June to September . <p> The United Nations Children 's Fund ( UNICEF ) has also projected that 2.6 million children under five will be affected by malnutrition this year , with one million at risk of severe acute malnutrition -- double the 2024 figure . <p> Conflict , insecurity , restricted access to farmland , extreme weather events , and rising food prices have compounded the crisis . Severe flooding is also forecast for 2025 , raising fears of further @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> In August , the NHF confirmed that it had mobilized $15.9 million in contributions this year , bringing its cumulative funding since 2017 to more than $215 million . Of this year 's total , $16.6 million has been allocated to four separate interventions benefiting over 970,000 people in the BAY states . <p> The allocations include $14.5 million for the 2025 Lean Season Multi-Sectoral Plan , which focuses on nutrition , health , water , sanitation , and protection services . The plan is designed to stabilize food security and reduce mortality through targeted partnerships with NGOs . Notably , 80 percent of the Standard Allocation ( SA1 ) of $4.5 million has been directed to national NGOs , reflecting a strong commitment to localization . <p> A further $2 million has been allocated to anticipatory action to mitigate projected flooding impacts in at-risk areas , building on lessons from the 2024 intervention . This allocation will provide multi-purpose cash assistance , early warning messaging , camp coordination and management support , and protection services , with implementation led entirely by local organizations . The funding follows a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if flood conditions shift beyond initially targeted locations . <p> The NHF also allocated $100,000 to restore emergency telecommunications in hard-to-reach areas , ensuring humanitarian access and coordination in zones cut off by insecurity or natural disasters . <p> Announcing the allocations , the NHF said its strategy is to place national NGOs and frontline responders at the center of the humanitarian response in Nigeria 's northeast . " Localization and accountability remain central to the Fund 's work , " it stated , emphasizing that locally-driven responses are more adaptive , cost-effective , and trusted by affected communities . <p> By prioritizing local capacity and partnerships , the NHF is seeking to avert a deepening humanitarian catastrophe in northeast Nigeria , where millions remain caught between conflict , hunger , and the worsening impacts of climate change .

@@128500429 <h> 2025 , the year of the mosquito <p> This year was actually named the year of the snake by the Chinese . It follows a pattern from several centuries where the Chinese name each particular year after an animal . However , this year may well have been named the Year of the Mosquito . <p> This energetic , highly irritating insect has long been considered a nuisance in many parts of the world . Now , it is increasingly being recognised as one of the most significant global public health threats of the 21st century . <p> These tiny insects , which have existed for millions of years , are transforming into increasingly efficient vectors of disease in our rapidly changing world . The concern surrounding mosquitoes is not merely about itchy bites but also about their accelerating capacity to transmit deadly pathogens to human populations . <p> This complex convergence of environmental , sociological , and biological factors has created what experts are calling " a warmer , sicker world " where mosquito-borne diseases are becoming more prevalent , more widespread , and more challenging to control.The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ expansion of mosquito-borne diseases . <p> As temperatures rise , mosquitoes can invade and thrive in habitats that were once too hostile for their survival . Unlike humans and other mammals , mosquitoes are cold-blooded creatures , meaning every aspect of their life cycle starting from biting rates to maturation speed , depends on external temperatures . Different mosquito species have different temperature preferences . For example , Aedes triseriatus thrives at temperatures as low as 22 ? C ( 72 ? F ) , while Aedes aegypti prefers to live around 29 ? C ( 84 ? F ) . As regions experience warmer conditions , these insects can expand their geographic ranges into new territories . The phenomenon is not limited to gradual temperature increases . Extreme weather events linked to climate change , which include droughts , heatwaves , floods , and unusual rainfall patterns , are creating ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes . Floodwaters pooling in small containers provide perfect nurseries for larvae , while droughts encourage water storage practices that inadvertently create additional breeding sites . Rapid urbanisation across tropical and subtropical regions , due mainly to economic growth , has created ideal conditions for mosquito proliferation , particularly for species like Aedes aegypti that thrive in human environments . The growth of cities has been accompanied by inadequate infrastructure , poor sewage control , leading to poor sanitation and abundant standing water in everything from discarded containers to improperly maintained drainage systems . Land use changes and human conflict , as we have witnessed with the Boko Haram insurgency , can also drive migration to cities , increasing the population at risk of explosive outbreaks . @@128500903 <p> Analysts have opined that exploring trade is remains an option to tackle food security <p> The world is not on track to end hunger , achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture by 2030 . Despite sustained reduction , global undernourishment has plateaued since 2020 and remains high . Progress towards eliminating hunger is slowing , particularly due to factors including conflict , economic crises , rising food prices and climate change , with Africa being especially impacted . <p> Trade plays a crucial role in combating food insecurity by facilitating the efficient movement of food from surplus to deficit regions , helping stabilize prices and improving access to a diverse and nutritious food supply -- particularly during local shortages or crises . <p> A recent issue note from UN Trade and Development ( UNCTAD ) underscores the potential of trade measures to mitigate food crises , as it examines the link between trade and food insecurity , with policy recommendations to support famine relief and strengthen global food security . <p> Trade is essential to reduce food insecurity <p> Trade is a fundamental component of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are traded in large volumes : approximately 25 per cent of global wheat , 14 per cent of maize and 10 per cent of rice production cross international borders each year . In many net food-importing developing countries , these import shares are significantly higher than the global averages . For instance , Egypt imports around 56 per cent of its wheat consumption . <p> Additionally , about 37 per cent of vegetable oils -- a major dietary calorie source -- are traded globally . In comparison , trade in all food items combined accounts for roughly 12 per cent of global production . <p> Most countries around the world are net importers of cereals , with only 34 nations currently classified as net exporters . This imbalance underscores the critical importance of a stable international trade system and the uninterrupted flow of cereals from surplus-producing countries . Trade is essential to meeting global demand and sustaining the livelihoods of millions . <p> Only a handful of countries export more cereals than they import , and even fewer maintain a significant export surplus . This concentration of export capacity makes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reliable access to foreign supplies , many regions would face food shortages , price volatility and increased vulnerability to climate-related crop failures or geopolitical disruptions . <p> In light of widespread dependence on imports and mentioned vulnerabilities , the report entitled " Trade against hunger " proposes a mechanism to combat severe food insecurity . It aims to enhance the export capacity and economic resilience of countries facing , or at risk of , severe food insecurity by temporarily eliminating tariffs with flexible rules of origin , supporting compliance with non-tariff measures , improving transport and logistics , as well as facilitating access to essential agricultural inputs to boost food security . <p> Imports are often concentrated among a limited number of suppliers , creating vulnerabilities when deliveries are disrupted due to conflict or extreme weather events . For example , Egypt -- a country heavily reliant on wheat imports -- sourced approximately 80 per cent of its wheat from Ukraine and the Russian Federation . <p> A positive example of international cooperation to reduce such disruptions is the set of agreements brokered by the United Nations and T ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the accompanying memorandum of understanding . Between July 2022 and July 2023 , these agreements played a key role in supporting global food security by enabling the continued export of food and fertilizers from Ukraine and the Russian Federation . As a result , the FAO Food Price Index fell by 23 per cent from its record high in March 2022 . <p> Access to fertilizers , most of which are imported , is another major challenge for efficient domestic food production . In 2023 , net food-importing developing countries spent nearly $2 billion on fertilizers . While crop prices such as those of cereals and soybeans declined , fertilizer prices remained elevated . Urea and potassium chloride prices rose by 18.5 per cent and 11.9 per cent , respectively , while diammonium phosphate ( DAP ) prices fluctuated . Compared to pre-pandemic levels in December 2019 , prices were still significantly higher : 26.6 per cent for urea , 148 per cent for potassium chloride and 75.7 per cent for DAP . <p> Countries that rely heavily on food imports must diversify their sources to reduce the risk and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extreme weather events become more frequent and marine logistics face growing constraints , it 's increasingly vital for nations to source strategic food commodities from a broader range of suppliers . <p> Trade plays a pivotal role in ensuring food security , particularly in agriculturally diverse economies such as those in North Africa . Countries with this profile should consider trade policy reforms that support both agrifood production and exports , as well as the import of essential agricultural inputs such as seeds , fertilizers and equipment . <p> However , high tariffs , tariff escalation and burdensome non-tariff measures remain significant obstacles to the development of regional agrifood value chains . These barriers not only hinder intra-regional trade but also limit the ability of neighbouring countries to build integrated agrifood systems , UN Trade and Development research warns . <p> In addition to market access obstacles , weak infrastructure poses a major challenge . <p> Investment in infrastructure is of crucial importance . To effectively combat acute food insecurity and the growing threat of famine , especially in vulnerable regions , there is an urgent need to invest in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ transport , logistics and compliance infrastructure to facilitate efficient food trade . Strengthening these systems will not only improve access to essential agricultural inputs like fertilizers but also enable the smoother movement of cereals and vegetable oils -- key components of global nutrition -- from surplus to deficit regions . <p> To address market access challenges , countries can collaborate to harmonize or mutually recognize standards and technical regulations . Greater regional integration -- facilitated through trade agreements -- can enhance trade facilitation and improve food availability . This is especially critical for perishable goods such as fruits , vegetables , dairy and meat , as well as strategic staples like wheat , which are particularly vulnerable to delays and high compliance costs at borders .

" <h> The multiple threats : how climate events affect menstrual well-being <p> The climate crisis affects menstrual health on multiple levels . This can generate nutritional deficiencies that impact menstrual health . Heat waves , on the other hand , can worsen menstrual pain and increase the risk of infections , as well as , as some studies suggest , cause hormonal imbalances . <p> Studies link air pollution to early puberty and irregular menstrual cycles . Society also overlooks and marginalises menstruating bodies , showing little awareness or consideration for their needs . Following extreme events , people often underestimate or completely ignore the needs of those menstruating . For example , a study in Pakistan notes that aid providers included tents , food , blankets , and mattresses among essential goods for displaced people but excluded hygienic and menstrual products . Listening to and addressing the needs of those directly affected , while continuing to investigate how the climate crisis impacts menstrual health . Meanwhile , 106 million people still drink directly from untreated surface water sources . <p> According to the findings , 3.4 billion people worldwide still lack safely managed sanitation , with 354 million practising open defecation , while 1.7 billion people lack basic hygiene services at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all . <h> Girls disproportionately affected <p> The data also highlighted the gendered burden of water access . <p> In many parts of sub-Saharan Africa and Central and Southern Asia , women and girls remain primarily responsible for water collection , with many spending more than 30 minutes daily fetching water . <p> A lack of safe water , sanitation and hygiene also has direct consequences for children 's health , education and development . Adolescent girls , in particular , face additional challenges during menstruation . <p> Data from 70 countries show that while most girls and women have some form of menstrual material and a private place to change , many can not change as often as necessary . <p> As a result , adolescent girls aged 15 -- 19 are less likely than adult women to participate fully in school , work and social activities during their periods . <h> Global goals at risk <p> With only five years left to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals ( SDGs ) , WHO and UNICEF warn that the target of universal coverage of safely managed water , sanitation and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Ruediger Krech , the acting director for environment , climate change and health at WHO , said water , sanitation and hygiene are not privileges but basic rights . <p> Mr Krech noted that urgent action is needed to close the gap for the world 's most vulnerable communities . <p> " We must accelerate action , especially for the most marginalised communities , if we are to keep our promise to reach the Sustainable Development Goals , " he said . <p> Similarly , Cecilia Scharp , the director of water , sanitation and hygiene at UNICEF , stressed that the absence of safe water places children at serious risk . <p> Ms Scharp noted that the situation has particularly dire consequences for girls , who are forced to shoulder the burden of water collection and face additional barriers during menstruation . <p> " When children lack access to safe water , sanitation , and hygiene , their health , education , and futures are put at risk . ( WASH ) refers to essential services that ensure access to safe drinking water , proper sanitation facilities , and the ability to practise good hygiene . <p> In 2018 , the federal government declared a state of emergency in the WASH sector , with an estimated 60 million people living without access to basic drinking water , according to the World Bank Group . <p> The World Bank noted that women and girls bear the burden of water collection , often walking long distances to fetch water , a task linked to school dropouts , poor health , and increased exposure to gender-based violence . <p> Further evidence from the 2021 WASH National Outcome Routine Mapping ( WASHNORM ) survey , conducted by the Federal Ministry of Water Resources and the National Bureau of Statistics with support from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ alarming picture . <p> The survey revealed that about 48 million Nigerians still practise open defecation , while only eight per cent of the population engage in safe handwashing . <p> In addition , 23 per cent of citizens do not have access to basic water supply services , and only 10 per cent have access to basic WASH services combined . <p> While modest progress has been made through initiatives such as the Clean Nigeria Campaign , experts warn that the country is unlikely to achieve its target of an open defecation-free Nigeria by 2025 without greater investment and political will . <p> The WASHNORM survey emphasised that collecting routine data is critical for evidence-based planning , budgeting , and resource mobilisation to accelerate Nigeria 's progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals on water and sanitation by 2030.

" <p> The NDCs , as most of us know are series of national commitments under Article 4.2 of the Paris Agreement on Climate Change , which represent countries ' pathways to climate action . <p> This is to be reviewed every five years and in line with these important stipulations , Parties to the Paris Agreement , Nigeria inclusive , are expected to develop and summit the third iteration of their national climate commitments known as Nationally Determined Contributions ( NDCs 3.0 ) before the end of this year . <p> The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change , adopted in 2015 , to limit global warming to well below 2 ? C , preferably 1.5 ? C , above pre-industrial levels . <p> A big commendation must of course go to all involved in the process of the development of Nigeria 's NDCs 3.0 because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were conscious efforts to engage everyone , even reaching out to subnational leaders to make their submissions.The importance of this effort at integrating subnational considerations in the development process of the NDCs can not be overemphasized . <p> This is because the devastation wrought by climate change in the form of destruction of infrastructure , loss of arable land due to land degradation , health challenges , insecurity , etc are ultimately borne by people within communities , local governments and states . In essence , the subnational . <p> They should therefore be critical to this.This was a point I re-iterated on the 3rd of June when the National Council on Climate Change came to brief my committee -- House of Representatives Committee on Climate Change and Security -- on our NDCs 3.0 process . <p> I made it clear to them that there was a need to also engage subnational legislators . These legislators have key roles to play.For instance , the draft NDCs 3.0 makes the case for eradication of generator use , support for a switch to clean cook options , etc . <p> None of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ federal " . @@128653567 <p> I still hear my mum 's voice echoing through the house : " No food wastage ! " If we had rice and stew on Monday , Tuesday 's lunch was sure to be what she called r ? chauff ? -- yesterday 's food , lovingly reimagined and reheated . As a child , I rolled my eyes and staged tantrums to avoid leftovers , but my mum stood firm : every grain had to be eaten . <p> What felt like punishment then , I now see as wisdom ; she was reducing waste , saving money , and teaching us to value food . She was not just a disciplinarian in the kitchen ; she was living out an ethic of environmental stewardship long before we had words like " climate action . " Like many women across Nigeria and beyond , she was shaping food systems and sustaining her family through everyday acts of care , an unsung environmental champion in her own right . <p> The Global Food Waste Crisis <p> Advertisement <p> What I once dismissed as a childhood inconvenience is today part @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ produce more food than we eat . The FAO 's landmark analysis estimates that roughly one-third of food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted , about 1.3 billion tonnes each year . The UNEP Food Waste Index 2024 estimates 631 million tonnes of household food waste in 2022 , more than one billion meals thrown away every single day , at a time when hundreds of millions of people face hunger . Consequently , the climate cost is enormous : food that is not eaten accounts for about 8 -- 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions , driven largely by methane released when organic waste decomposes in landfills and dumpsites . Methane is a short-lived but highly potent climate pollutant ; over a 20-year period , one tonne of methane traps about 80 times more heat than one tonne of CO2 . This makes food waste not just a waste management issue , but a fast-acting driver of climate change . <p> This is why I see r ? chauff ? -- the practice of reinventing leftovers , not as an afterthought , but as climate action from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it would stand among the top emitters . But the most elegant solution is also the simplest : eat what you have . The United Nations and leading analysts have repeatedly identified reducing food waste ( alongside shifting toward plant-rich diets ) as among the most impactful climate actions available to ordinary people and communities . Each time we finish what we cook or transform yesterday 's stew into today 's fresh lunch , we cut emissions from decomposition and avoid the need to produce replacement meals . <p> Why Women Must Be at the Centre <p> There 's another truth we must state clearly : kitchen-based climate action is gendered . " Globally , women , especially in low- and middle-income countries , play a leading role in managing food preparation , purchasing , and preservation . In Nigeria , women are often the decision-makers on how food is cooked , stored , and shared . That means empowering women with knowledge and tools for climate-smart cooking ( like leftover reuse and plant-based diversification ) can unlock enormous climate co-benefits . " Beyond norms , this is also about @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ day on unpaid care and domestic work than men , a gap that persists worldwide and shapes who does the daily work of preventing food waste at home . Looks Like <p> Eat what you have : Plan portions realistically , store leftovers promptly , and use them within days . Food safety authorities advise refrigerating leftovers within two hours , eating them within 3 -- 4 days , or freezing them for longer . Always reheat to 74 -- 75 ? C / 165 ? F until steaming hot . <p> Stretch with plants : Turn yesterday 's rice or stew into a new dish by adding vegetables , legumes , or leafy greens . This not only boosts nutrition but also lowers the meal 's carbon footprint compared with adding more meat . <p> Mind methane : Every portion rescued from the bin is one less contribution to methane emissions . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ each avoided scrap matters . <p> These may seem like small actions , but multiplied across millions of kitchens , they reduce emissions , ease strain on family budgets , and contribute to global climate goals . <p> Eat What You Have : Normalise and promote the culture of consuming what is already cooked or purchased before preparing new meals . Schools , media , and community campaigns can champion this ethic , turning it into a collective climate practice rather than just a household rule . Eating what we have reduces waste , saves money , and strengthens food security . <p> Recognise leadership : Put women at the centre of food programs and climate policy as educators , innovators , and decision-makers . <p> Conclusion <p> I think back to my mother , to the way her r ? chauff ? meals were never second-class , always hot , garnished , and nourishing . @@128730360 <h> 5% surcharge : A golden opportunity to wean Nigeria off its fossil fuel addiction <p> Nigeria , Africa 's largest oil producer , has announced a 5% tax on all fossil fuel sales as part of its new tax law that goes into effect in January 2026 . According to this new tax regulation , Nigerians are now expected to pay a " 5% surcharge that is chargeable on fossil fuel products provided or produced in Nigeria " , a fee which , according to the stipulation of the act , " shall be collected at the time of a chargeable transaction , meaning at the point of sale " . This surcharge excludes clean or renewable energy products , household kerosene , cooking gas , and compressed natural gas ( CNG ) . <p> The framing and the wording of this law make it an effort to put a price incentive on fossil fuel consumption , to shift consumption from fossil fuels to cleaner alternatives . This , in every sense , mirrors a carbon tax , even though in this case , a percentage was used instead @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , a carbon tax is a sales tax applicable to fossil fuels or carbon-intensive fuels at the point of purchase . Depending on the country or jurisdiction , the primary aim of a carbon tax is to disincentivise the use of fossil fuels and , secondarily , to raise revenue for the government . This is known as the double dividend of carbon pricing . <p> Let us start with what the government of the day has got right . First , the surcharge or fossil fuel tax was not introduced in isolation . The tax was introduced as part of a broader framework of tax reforms , drawing inspiration from how Sweden introduced its carbon tax in the 1990s as part of a broader comprehensive tax reform . Such an approach helps reduce the risk of backlash and the possibility of the tax being struck down before it even takes off . Embedding the surcharge in a cocktail of tax policies insulates it from undue scrutiny . In the same vein , implementing the surcharge alongside other reforms ensures that the policy is in sync with other new regulations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Advertisement <p> Nigeria 's 5% surcharge is a brilliant effort to wean the country off its long-term addiction to fossil fuels . This policy demonstrates proactive thinking and fiscal foresight on the part of the government . If done properly , it has the potential of helping to help decouple Nigeria 's economic growth from carbon emissions , actualise its NDC commitment , and mobilise finance for sustainable development . This comes after the government removed the problematic fuel subsidy two years ago , an effort that , coupled with the recent surge in electricity tariff , has led to an accelerated renewable energy adoption and an explosion in solar uptake . As a result , the country moved to 4th place in Africa for solar energy adoption in 2024 with an addition of 63.5 MWp of capacity , bringing its total installed capacity to 385.7 MWp as people scrambled to find cheaper alternative sources of energy . <p> The new tax policy , even though a brilliant emissions mitigation and revenue generation tool , is not without flaws . Applying a 5% flat rate on fossil fuels disregards @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rapidly shrinking middle class . It does n't seem fair that both the rich and the poor in the poverty capital of the world should have to pay the same tax on fossil fuels . At best , a progressive surcharge that increases with a certain threshold would have been more practical for a country where millions of households and Small and Medium Scale Enterprises ( SMEs ) rely on petrol-powered generators to power their homes and businesses . <p> Fairness aside , there is also a big question mark about revenue utilisation . The 2025 Tax Act does not spell out or imply what happens to the revenue generated from the fossil fuel surcharge . While preliminary analysis suggests that this policy is more revenue-driven than environmentally motivated intervention , it is essential that the government clearly outlines how the revenue from the tax will be used . Sweden and British Columbia adopted a revenue-neutral approach to their carbon tax , which meant that the carbon tax essentially returned to citizens through tax cuts , rebates , and climate windfall payouts . Even though the Nigeria Act Law of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of them is directly related or designed to act as a cushion or corollary to the 5% fossil fuel tax . <p> Advertisement <p> Global best practices demand that a policy like this in a sensitive sector like energy should be accompanied by a clear framework for revenue monitoring , reporting , and utilisation to foster transparency and build citizens ' trust . The masses deserve to know that the surcharge is being deployed to finance the transition to a green , just , and cleaner future . The revenue from the tax could be used to replenish the climate fund and run the activities of the National Climate Change Council Secretariat ( NCCCS ) , which is part of the provisions of the Climate Change Act of 2021 . Rather than wait for foreign loans or grants , this tax could also help kick-start comprehensive nature-based adaptation efforts and finance resilience building through research and development in green technologies like batteries , electric vehicles , and charging stations . <p> The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) estimates that emerging economies and developing countries , minus China @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate and nature-related investments , plus an additional US$3 trillion to achieve the other Sustainable Development Goals . We have a mountain of deficit to climb ; closing the climate finance gap requires innovative thinking that does not put us at the mercy of developed nations . As with every other climate policy , this one is not without pain , but if done effectively , the gain in the long run will eclipse the short-term pain . In Denmark , electric vehicles were the best-selling cars of 2024 , all thanks to an established market-driven price incentive policy that made it more attractive for people to move away from fossil fuel-powered cars to cleaner alternatives . <p> The famous Newton 's First Law of Motion states that a body remains at a state of rest or in uniform motion except it is acted upon by an external force . For decades , Nigeria has remained in a state of rest and uniform motion , content to keep pumping and gulping fossil fuels , but all indications suggest that fossil fuels are not the future , and it is time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that will compel us down the right path to a future beyond oil .
